nameStory: This moss gets its 'wavy-leaf' name from the distinctive undulating edges of its leaves that ripple like tiny green waves when you look closely. The scientific name 'ciliare' means 'fringed with hairs,' referring to the fine teeth along those wavy leaf margins that look like delicate eyelashes under magnification.
description: Wavy-leaf Moss is a medium-sized moss that forms loose, bright green carpets in shaded woodland areas. Individual plants grow in small rosettes or loose tufts, typically reaching about half an inch to an inch tall. The leaves are relatively large for a moss, oval-shaped with those characteristic wavy, toothed edges that give this species its distinctive appearance. When conditions are right, it produces capsules on slender stalks that arch gracefully above the leafy shoots.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval leaves with distinctly wavy, toothed margins that feel slightly rough to gentle touch - run your finger along a leaf edge and you'll feel the tiny teeth

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms loose, scattered tufts or thin mats rather than dense cushions - individual rosettes are easily distinguished from each other

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Bright yellowish-green when moist, becoming duller olive-green when dry - one of the more vibrant woodland mosses

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Leaves feel relatively thick and substantial for a moss, with a slightly glossy surface that catches light when wet

idTips.label: Sporophytes
idTips.description: Egg-shaped capsules on curved stalks that nod downward when mature, appearing in late spring to early summer

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Almost always found on rich, moist soil in deciduous woods, rarely on logs or rocks like many other mosses

habitat: Look for Wavy-leaf Moss on rich, moist soil in deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England, especially in areas with maple, beech, and birch trees. It prefers shaded spots with consistent moisture and good leaf litter, often growing along stream banks, in ravines, or on gentle slopes where organic matter accumulates. Unlike many mosses, it rarely colonizes rocks or fallen logs, showing a strong preference for earthy substrates.

seasonality.spring: Most vibrant and easily spotted as it responds to increased moisture - sporophytes begin developing their characteristic curved stalks and capsules during late spring.
seasonality.summer: Continues active growth in shaded areas, with mature capsules releasing spores by midsummer before withering away.
seasonality.fall: Remains green and identifiable as leaves accumulate around it, though it becomes less prominent without sporophytes present.
seasonality.winter: Stays green under snow cover but appears somewhat dulled - still identifiable by leaf characteristics on mild winter days.

funFact: Each tiny leaf of Wavy-leaf Moss has a single prominent vein running down its center that acts like a miniature water highway, efficiently moving moisture from the leaf tip down to the stem - you can actually see this 'moss spine' with just a magnifying glass!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other thyme-mosses in the same genus, but the wavy leaf edges are your best clue - run your finger gently along a leaf margin and you'll feel the rippled, toothed edge that other similar mosses lack. Memory trick: 'Wavy leaves, wavy edges!'
contextualKnowledge: The name 'thyme-moss' for this genus is somewhat misleading since these mosses are unrelated to culinary thyme and don't smell like herbs at all. The name comes from early botanists who thought the small, oval leaves resembled those of thyme plants, though the connection is purely visual.
compareHints: Wavy-leaf Moss stands out from its thyme-moss relatives primarily by those distinctive wavy, toothed leaf margins - Woodsy Thyme-moss has smoother leaf edges, while Marsh Thyme-moss prefers wetter areas and has more pointed leaves. Alpine thyme-moss is much smaller overall and typically found at higher elevations, making habitat a good distinguishing feature.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its thyme-moss relatives, Woodsy Thyme-moss has the most orderly, shingle-like leaf arrangement compared to Wavy-leaf Moss's more irregular, wavy-edged leaves.
Unlike its relatives Woodsy Thyme-moss (found in forests) and Marsh Thyme-moss (found in wetlands), Alpine thyme-moss is strictly a high-elevation specialist.
Compared to its relatives, Marsh Thyme-moss has the broadest, most elliptical leaves - Woodsy Thyme-moss has more pointed leaves, while Wavy-leaf Moss has distinctly wavy leaf edges.
